newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss National Bank says it trusted Nazis on gold.
newsitem.headline: Swiss National Bank says it trusted Nazis on gold.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) acknowledged on Friday that it acted with considerable credulousness towards Hitler's Germany in buying Nazi gold during World War Two that might have been stolen.
The SNB noted it had made the same acknowledgment in 1985 and was repeating it now after a British Foreign Office report this week rekindled speculation about the whereabouts of Nazi wealth.

An SNB statement, based on a 1985 study published by the bank, said the wartime bank acted with no consideration for the political situation in buying over 1.2 billion Swiss francs in gold from Hitler's Reichsbank central bank.
During the war, the Allies cautioned Switzerland that Germany was looting gold from the countries and peoples it had conquered.
"In its transactions with the German Reichsbank, the (SNB) board manifested considerable credulousness," the statement said.

The SNB said it welcomed efforts by the Swiss government and parliament, which are preparing a commission for a broad inquiry into wartime Swiss banking, dealings with Nazi Germany and lost accounts of Jews murdered in the Holocaust.
"The relevant documents in the archives of the Swiss National bank remain open to the public," the statement said.

Switzerland's sedate banking and political establishments have been shocked into launching inquiries into wartime events by mounting international claims that Swiss banks were still hoarding wealth left by Nazis and Holocaust victims.

The SNB statement said its governing board, the policy-making body headed by president Hans Meyer, had briefed the bank's supervisory council about the Nazi gold issue at the council's regular quarterly meeting on Friday.
"The governing board spoke with the council about the issue because it has received so much international coverage this week, especially in the British media," an SNB spokesman said.

The British Foreign Office revived interest in the fate of Nazi treasure with a report this week that summarised previously public documents, including allegations that Switzerland gave just over one-tenth of Nazi gold back to the Allies after 1945.

Switzerland agreed in Washington in 1946 to pay the Allies 250 million Swiss francs (about $60 million at the time) as compensation for buying Nazi gold that may have been stolen from German-occupied countries or Holocaust victims.
This week's British report alleged Switzerland had brought over $500 million dollars in gold from Germany, a number that historians said was somewhat higher than previously known.
The SNB made clear on Friday it saw no more legal ramifications of the Nazi gold deals after the 1946 deal with the United States, Britain and France.
"As far as legal aspects of the gold transactions are concerned, a settlement was reached with the 1946 agreement between the Allies and Switzerland in Washington," it said.
